strengths: Novel and clearly motivated direction: G2P is, to the authors' knowledge, the first method to directly transfer aligned 3DGS attributes (scale, opacity) to point-level segmentation in native 3D space, avoiding point-to-pixel misalignment issues of 2D-3D fusion, and is positioned clearly against both boundary-aware and cross-modal fusion lines of work.

Technically sensible design: covariance-aware (Mahalanobis) Gaussian-to-point matching that accounts for anisotropic ellipsoids is a reasonable and well-justified solution to the misalignment between optimized Gaussians and original point geometry; the distillation design keeps Gaussian features out of the inference path.

Consistent empirical gains across multiple benchmarks: +1.4 mIoU over PT v3 on ScanNet v2, +2.1 on ScanNet200, +0.8 on ScanNet++, +0.4 on Matterport3D, plus competitive ScanNet200 hidden-test results, with clear per-class improvements on geometrically challenging classes (refrigerator +6.0, shower curtain +7.2).

Thorough ablations: component-wise ablation, comparison of appearance-transfer strategies (raw Gaussians vs. opacity inputs vs. distillation), distance metric and neighborhood size k, and training/inference efficiency analysis (inference overhead is modest in latency and parameters).
Fair comparison discipline: baselines are reproduced under identical settings, external pre-training usage is explicitly flagged, and code release is promised.
weaknesses: The overall margin is modest (+1.4 mIoU over the strongest reproduced geometric baseline) and no variance/significance analysis is provided; given that reproduced PT v3 numbers are used, seed-to-seed variability could affect conclusions. The headline 'geometrically challenging' class grouping is author-defined and post-hoc, and results within that group are mixed (picture IoU actually drops from 41.8 to 39.4 vs. PT v3; curtain improves only +0.1).

Attribution of gains is somewhat entangled with existing components: the backbone is PT v3 and the boundary head adopts BFANet's B-S block, so part of the improvement over BFANet may stem from backbone differences rather than the proposed GS-guided signals; an ablation of the B-S block alone (PT v3 + B-S without GS-derived labels) is missing to fully isolate the contribution.

The claim of operating 'without any 2D or language supervision' is somewhat overstated: the pipeline depends on pre-computed 3DGS reconstructions (SceneSplat-7K), which themselves require multi-view imagery; applicability to scenes without images or to outdoor scenes (explicitly unavailable) is not addressed, and no limitations section discusses this dependency.

The boundary pseudo-label pipeline introduces several heuristic choices (trimming ratio η=0.7, semantic radius r=4cm, background-class exclusion) with no sensitivity analysis; noise/robustness of labels derived from noisy GS reconstructions (acknowledged by the authors as having 'indistinct edges') is not quantified.

An unexplained inference-side memory increase of +74% (1.9GB to 3.3GB) despite Gaussian features being removed at inference is noted but not analyzed; combined with +67% training latency, the practical cost should be characterized more carefully.

The appearance encoder requires a separate 400-epoch from-scratch pre-training per dataset on separate hardware, increasing total training cost; this overhead is not included in the efficiency discussion.

Presentation issues: Fig. 2 is dense and hard to parse; details of the appearance encoder pre-training objective (how Sonata's self-supervised framework is adapted to learn from opacity) are deferred and under-specified in the main text; no qualitative failure cases or societal-impact discussion are provided.

strengths: The core idea is reasonably original and well-motivated: transferring 3D Gaussian Splatting attributes (opacity, scale) to point clouds via anisotropy-aware Mahalanobis matching is a clean way to inject appearance cues into geometry-only segmentation without 2D-3D projection losses.

The evaluation is fairly broad: ScanNet v2 (val + class-wise split), ScanNet200 (val + hidden test), ScanNet++, and Matterport3D, plus ablations on the correspondence metric/neighborhood size (Tab. 8), appearance transfer strategy (Tab. 7), and inference efficiency (Tab. 9).

The ablations are informative: Tab. 7 shows direct use of raw Gaussians fails (73.1 mIoU) while distillation works, and Tab. 8 supports covariance-aware matching over Euclidean distance, lending credibility to the design choices.
The pipeline requires no Gaussian features at inference time, and the efficiency analysis (Tab. 9) honestly reports the training overhead (+67% latency, +30% memory), which is good practice.

The class-wise analysis (Tab. 2) and qualitative results (Fig. 4) are aligned with the claimed mechanism, showing gains specifically on geometrically challenging classes such as refrigerator and shower curtain.
weaknesses: The headline gains are modest: +1.4 mIoU over the reproduced PT v3 baseline on ScanNet v2, +0.8 on ScanNet++, and only +0.4 on Matterport3D. On the ScanNet200 hidden test set (Tab. 4), G2P actually underperforms BFANet (35.5 vs 36.0 mIoU), which weakens the 'superior performance on standard benchmarks' claim.

The framing 'without any 2D or language supervision' is somewhat misleading: the Gaussian attributes are obtained from SceneSplat-7K GS reconstructions that are fitted to posed multi-view RGB imagery. Appearance information is therefore derived from 2D images indirectly, and the method introduces a substantial extra dependency (GS reconstruction of every training scene, ~1.5M primitives each) that is not compared against simply using the source images in a 2D-3D fusion baseline under equivalent conditions.

The component ablation (Tab. 5) shows each module alone yields only +0.8 mIoU (77.8) with no OA gain, and the combined gain is +1.4; such small margins on a 1201-scene validation set warrant statistical significance analysis or multiple seeds, which are not reported.

Heavy reliance on existing components: the backbone (PT v3), the boundary-semantic block (BFANet), and the teacher architecture (Sonata, repurposed) are all borrowed, so the net novelty is confined to the attribute alignment and pseudo-label generation. Notation is also sloppy in Sec. 3.4/4.1: Eq. 5 defines a threshold τη, but the implementation section sets 'the scale-based trimming ratio τη = 0.7' while the text describes a percentage η — the threshold-vs-ratio terminology is inconsistent.

Not all classes improve: 'picture' IoU drops (39.4 vs 41.8 for PT v3) and several distinguishable classes are essentially flat, suggesting the geometric-challenging-class narrative is not uniformly supported.

Boundary pseudo-labels are partly derived from ground-truth semantic labels (B_sem uses neighboring semantic labels), and no analysis is given of robustness to imperfect GS reconstructions or how the method would behave on scenes without reliable posed imagery, which limits the claimed generality.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated direction: G2P is, to my knowledge, the first method to explicitly align optimized 3DGS attributes (opacity, scale) with point clouds for point-level semantic segmentation, addressing the geometric-bias problem without 2D images or language supervision.

Technically sound correspondence design: the Mahalanobis-distance-based point-to-Gaussian matching (Eq. 1-3) is a principled way to handle anisotropic splats, and the ablation in Tab. 8 clearly supports it over Euclidean matching.

Comprehensive experimental evidence: evaluations span ScanNet v2, ScanNet200 (val + hidden test), ScanNet++, and Matterport3D, with class-wise analysis of geometrically challenging categories (refrigerator +6.0, shower curtain +7.2 IoU over PT v3), component ablations (Tab. 5), appearance-transfer strategy comparisons (Tab. 7), and an inference-efficiency analysis (Tab. 9).

The distillation design is attractive in practice: Gaussian attributes are needed only at training time, so the inference model retains the standard point-cloud input and adds only 0.2M parameters, keeping the method deployable.
Appropriate attribution: the paper clearly credits SceneSplat-7K, Sonata, PT v3, and BFANet's B-S block, and honestly labels reproduced baselines (†) and methods using external pre-training (*).
weaknesses: Overall gains are modest and inconsistent with the SOTA claim: +0.8 mIoU on ScanNet++ and +0.4 on Matterport3D are small, and on the ScanNet200 hidden test (Tab. 4) G2P (35.5) is below BFANet (36.0). The abstract/introduction claim of consistently superior performance is somewhat overreached; the text should be softened accordingly.

The 'geometrically challenging vs. distinguishable' class partition (Tab. 2) appears hand-crafted and post-hoc, which risks cherry-picking a grouping that flatters the method; the selection criteria for the two groups should be formalized or validated.

Partially a composition of existing components: the backbone (PT v3), boundary-semantic block (BFANet), teacher architecture (Sonata), and GS reconstructions (SceneSplat-7K) are all reused, so the isolated contribution is the attribute alignment/augmentation and its training signals; ablation (a) vs. (b) shows boundary guidance alone (using only the semantic part of the pseudo-labels) already gives +0.8, making the uniquely Gaussian contribution appear as ~+0.6-1.4 mIoU.

The scale-based boundary pseudo-label threshold is described as a dynamic top-η% trimming rule (Eq. 5, τη), yet the implementation states τη = 0.7 without clarifying the semantics; also B_sem uses ground-truth semantic labels, making the merged boundary supervision partially label-derived rather than purely a GS-derived pseudo-label, which should be discussed.

Applicability is limited to indoor scenes with available GS reconstructions (SceneSplat-7K is indoor-only); the paper does not discuss robustness to GS reconstruction quality, noise in opacity/scale attributes, or the cost of running 3DGS optimization as a preprocessing step.

The interpretation of opacity as 'view-consistent appearance' deserves more analysis: opacity primarily encodes visibility/blending contribution and can be entangled with floaters and reconstruction artifacts; a qualitative or quantitative failure analysis is missing.
No code is released at submission time ('will be released soon'), which limits reproducibility verification of the alignment and distillation pipeline.

strengths: The paper explores a novel and sensible direction: rather than fusing 2D image features (with the well-known projection/occlusion misalignment issues) or using noisy optimized Gaussians directly as segmentation input, it transfers GS-derived attributes (scale, opacity) onto the original point cloud geometry via a covariance-aware (Mahalanobis) alignment. This design cleanly separates geometric fidelity (points) from auxiliary appearance/visibility cues (Gaussians) and is a thoughtful response to a real limitation of both 2D-3D fusion and GS-direct approaches.

The Gaussian-free inference property is a practical strength: all Gaussian computation (GS reconstruction, augmentation, boundary extraction, teacher training) is confined to an offline preparation stage, and the distilled model consumes only points at test time. The cost analysis (Tab. 13) transparently quantifies this offline overhead.

Experimental evidence is comprehensive: four benchmarks (ScanNet v2, ScanNet200 including hidden test set, ScanNet++, Matterport3D), instance segmentation evaluation, class-wise analysis on geometrically challenging categories, and a rich set of ablations (module ablation, boundary pseudo-label sources, distance metric and neighborhood size, loss weights, attribute choices including SH/rotation exclusion, pruning ratio sensitivity). The ablations genuinely support each design decision.

The supplementary analysis (attribute distribution visualizations, PCA of teacher features, mIoU-PSNR correlation) provides convincing mechanistic support for interpreting scale as a boundary cue and opacity as a visibility-confidence cue, and honestly reports that G2P is not strongly dependent on GS reconstruction quality.

Limitations (offline preparation stage, indoor-only, GS availability) are stated clearly, and no claim of 2D/language-free superiority is overextended: the paper positions the method as 'competitive without external pre-training,' which is fair.
The manuscript is well written, clearly structured, and the two-stage pipeline (preparation + distillation-based training) is easy to follow.
weaknesses: The headline quantitative gains are modest: +0.9 mIoU over the PT v3 baseline and +0.4 over BFANet on ScanNet v2 (78.4), and G2P actually falls below BFANet on the ScanNet200 hidden test set (35.7 vs 36.0). Ablation Tab. 7 shows each component alone contributes only ~+0.8 mIoU, so the contribution rests on small but consistent margins; the evidence is adequate but the improvement size limits the impact claim.

Part of the gain may come from the boundary-guidance machinery (B-S block from BFANet, boundary supervision) rather than the GS cues themselves: Tab. 17 shows boundary supervision without distillation already reaches 77.8 from a 77.0 baseline, so the GS-distillation component contributes only ~+0.6 on top of a strong boundary-aware baseline. A cleaner attribution of the gain to the core 'Gaussian-to-Point alignment' idea would strengthen the paper.

The framing of opacity as an 'appearance' cue is somewhat overstated. The method deliberately excludes SH/color from the Gaussians, so the transferred cues (scale, opacity) are better described as structural/visibility signals; the claimed mitigation of 'geometric bias via appearance' is therefore weaker in principle than the introduction suggests, even if empirically effective for classes like refrigerator and shower curtain.

Heavy dependence on expensive offline preprocessing: 22 min/scene for GS optimization plus 27.9 h/dataset for teacher training. Although inference is Gaussian-free, the requirement that every new scene have a GS reconstruction (with per-dataset teacher training) limits applicability compared to plug-and-play 2D fusion, and the method is restricted to indoor scenes where SceneSplat-7K reconstructions exist. The limitation is acknowledged, but this is a substantive practical constraint.

The categorization of ScanNet v2 classes into 'geometrically challenging' vs 'distinguishable' is somewhat ad hoc and post-hoc; the strongest results are presented on this self-defined split, which slightly inflates the perceived advantage.

Reproduced baselines are slightly lower than reported numbers (PT v3 77.0 vs 77.5 official), which makes the +0.9 improvement over the baseline partially relative to a weaker reproduction, though comparisons against BFANet reproduced at its published parity partially offset this concern.
Memory at inference increases by +74% over PT v3 (Tab. 11), which is a non-trivial efficiency cost that is somewhat downplayed in the text compared to the training-cost discussion.

strengths: The core idea — transferring Gaussian opacity and scale attributes to point clouds via covariance-aware (Mahalanobis) matching while preserving original point geometry — is a sensible and reasonably novel direction, and the paper clearly differentiates itself from GS-rendering-based segmentation works and from UniPre3D-style pre-training.

The experimental evaluation is broad and honest: ScanNet v2, ScanNet200, ScanNet++, Matterport3D, a hidden-test-set result, and instance segmentation, with a large set of ablations (attribute choice, distillation vs. direct input, boundary pseudo-label sources, neighborhood size, loss weights) that support the design decisions.

The distillation formulation is well motivated: Gaussian-free inference is achieved, and Table 9/Table 14 show that the gain is not merely from distillation itself but from GS-derived attributes (a color/normal teacher underperforms the baseline).

The supplementary material is substantive: preparation-cost analysis, PSNR–mIoU correlation analysis, boundary pseudo-label visualizations, and a candid limitations discussion (offline pipeline, indoor-only, GS dependency).
weaknesses: The overall gains are marginal and the contribution is incremental. On ScanNet v2 the full method achieves 78.4 vs. 77.5 for the PT v3 baseline (+0.9), and the components are individually modest: boundary guidance alone +0.8 and distillation alone +0.8 (Table 7). Crucially, the boundary branch is borrowed wholesale from BFANet, so the novel GS-specific component contributes roughly +0.5–0.6 mIoU. On ScanNet200 hidden test the method actually trails BFANet (35.7 vs. 36.0), and instance segmentation gains are within noise. The headline results fall below the acceptance bar for a method paper whose practical cost is significantly higher than the baseline.

The central motivation — avoiding cross-modal 2D-3D fusion — is weaker than claimed. The Gaussian attributes (opacity, scale) are products of photometric optimization over posed multi-view images (SceneSplat-7K reconstructions). Appearance information is therefore still sourced from images; the pipeline merely replaces explicit projection with an offline GS reconstruction that costs ~22 minutes per scene plus 27.9 h of teacher training per dataset. The practical trade-off versus lightweight 2D-3D fusion is not analyzed.

The pipeline complexity and assumptions limit applicability: G2P requires pre-computed GS reconstructions aligned with the point cloud, works only indoors (no outdoor GS available), and the paper does not demonstrate behavior when GS reconstruction quality is poor beyond a coarse PSNR correlation. This constrains the significance of the contribution relative to geometry-only baselines that need no auxiliary reconstruction.

Efficiency claims are muddied: although inference is described as Gaussian-free, inference memory rises by +74% over PT v3 and latency by +21% (Table 11), and the comparison uses self-reproduced baseline numbers without clarifying discrepancies (e.g., BFANet reported 78.0 in the original paper but 77.3 reproduced).

The 'boundary-aware' framing oversells novelty: the boundary supervision machinery (B-S block, BCE+Dice boundary loss) is adopted from BFANet, and the scale-based pseudo-labels only provide a complementary cue whose best-case contribution over the semantic boundary variant is small (Table 8: 77.8 combined vs. 76.9 semantic-only, under a no-distillation setting).

Several important questions remain unaddressed: sensitivity to Gaussian reconstruction fidelity per scene, behavior on scenes without reliable GS (fallback strategy is only briefly described), and statistical significance of the sub-1-mIoU gains (no variance over seeds).

strengths: Novel and well-motivated direction: instead of 2D-3D projection or GS-rendered segmentation, the paper establishes explicit Gaussian-to-Point correspondences and transfers Gaussian opacity/scale attributes as auxiliary cues to a standard point cloud backbone, an alternative to 2D-3D fusion that avoids projection misalignment.

Technically sensible design choices: preserving original point geometry while using GS attributes only as auxiliary signals, covariance-aware (Mahalanobis) matching for anisotropic Gaussians (validated in Tab. 10 and Fig. 7), and distillation into a Gaussian-free point-only backbone so inference requires no GS data (Tab. 9).

Comprehensive evaluation: four benchmarks (ScanNet v2, ScanNet200 with hidden test set, ScanNet++, Matterport3D), instance segmentation transfer, class-wise analysis of geometrically challenging categories, and extensive ablations covering components, attribute choices, hyperparameters, and loss weights.

Thorough supplementary analysis, including attribute-distribution visualization (scale vs. opacity vs. rotation), PSNR-vs-mIoU correlation analysis, feature PCA analysis, preparation-stage cost accounting, and an honest limitations section (offline GS dependency, indoor-only scope).

Clear contribution framing consistent with an Algorithms/General contribution: the value lies in the alignment/distillation pipeline and the demonstrated usefulness of GS attributes for point-level segmentation, not in claiming a new state-of-the-art algorithm; the paper appropriately claims 'competitive' rather than superior overall performance.
weaknesses: Absolute gains are modest: +0.9 mIoU over PT v3 and +0.4 over the reproduced BFANet on ScanNet v2, and it does not surpass BFANet on the ScanNet200 hidden test set (35.7 vs. 36.0). Part of the gain likely comes from the adopted BFANet boundary-semantic block rather than the GS cues themselves; a BFANet+scale-pseudo-label-only baseline (without GS distillation) would sharpen the attribution, though Tab. 7 partially addresses this.

Heavy dependency on pre-existing GS reconstructions (SceneSplat-7K) and a per-dataset Sonata-style teacher trained from scratch (27.9 h/dataset plus 22 min/scene GS optimization), limiting applicability to settings without GS reconstructions and to indoor scenes only; the offline preparation cost is disclosed but weakens the practical claim of 'without pretrained 2D features'.

The 'geometrically challenging' vs. 'distinguishable' class grouping used for the headline class-wise analysis is hand-defined; a quantitative, criterion-based definition (or evaluation on a benchmark with such a split, e.g., ScanNet200 head/common/tail, which is included but shows G2P behind BFANet overall) would strengthen the core claim.

Statistical significance and variance are not reported; with gains of 0.4-1.4 mIoU, single-run results on the validation split (no test-set evaluation for the main benchmarks) leave uncertainty about robustness of the improvements.

Some tension in the narrative: the paper claims to mitigate 'geometric bias' via appearance, yet the transferred attributes (opacity, scale) are geometric/visibility signals rather than true appearance (color/texture is explicitly the point cloud's own input), which slightly overstates the mechanism; the opacity-based teacher is well supported empirically, but the framing could be more precise.

Reproducibility is plausible but not yet demonstrated: no code release is mentioned, and the pipeline couples multiple external components (SceneSplat-7K, Sonata, PT v3, BFANet blocks) whose interaction details matter.
